items.stem: Which of the following best describes the claim Luther makes in theses 42 through 46 of the excerpt?

options.text: Charity toward the needy does more spiritual good than buying pardons
options.why: Theses 43 and 44 say that giving to the poor is 'a better work than buying pardons' because 'love grows by works of love,' while pardons only free a person from penalty.
options.label: key

options.text: Buying pardons is itself a kind of almsgiving, since the money funds church buildings that serve the poor
options.why: Thesis 42 denies that buying pardons can be compared to works of mercy, and thesis 45 says neglecting the needy to buy pardons earns God's indignation.
options.label: reversal

options.text: The pope has no authority over purgatory and should be resisted by German princes and their subjects
options.why: Thesis 42 actually says what the pope 'does not intend,' which treats papal intent as sound. The excerpt calls on no one to resist the pope.
options.label: overstated

options.text: Christians are justified by faith alone, so good works and sacraments are useless for their salvation
options.why: Luther did later stress justification by faith, but this excerpt praises works of mercy and never calls good works or sacraments useless.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Charity toward the needy does more spiritual good than buying pardons". Theses 43 and 44 say that giving to the poor is 'a better work than buying pardons' because 'love grows by works of love,' while pardons only free a person from penalty.
"Buying pardons is itself a kind of almsgiving, since the money funds church buildings that serve the poor" is incorrect: Thesis 42 denies that buying pardons can be compared to works of mercy, and thesis 45 says neglecting the needy to buy pardons earns God's indignation.
"The pope has no authority over purgatory and should be resisted by German princes and their subjects" is incorrect: Thesis 42 actually says what the pope 'does not intend,' which treats papal intent as sound. The excerpt calls on no one to resist the pope.
"Christians are justified by faith alone, so good works and sacraments are useless for their salvation" is incorrect: Luther did later stress justification by faith, but this excerpt praises works of mercy and never calls good works or sacraments useless.
facts: Luther wrote the Ninety-Five Theses in 1517 to dispute the practice of indulgences.
An indulgence was understood to remit temporal punishment for sin, including in purgatory.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Theses 43-44 rank giving to the poor above buying pardons and explain that works of love make a person better.
design.evidence_quote: he who gives to the poor or lends to the needy does a better work than buying pardons

items.stem: Luther's criticism of preachers who promised that a coin in the money-box frees a soul (theses 27-28) was most directly a response to which of the following?

options.text: Henry VIII's dissolution of English monasteries and his sale of their lands to the gentry
options.why: The dissolution happened in the late 1530s, in England, and had nothing to do with indulgence preaching in Germany in 1517.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The Peace of Augsburg's grant to German princes of the right to choose their territory's faith
options.why: The Peace of Augsburg came in 1555, as a result of the religious conflict that Luther's challenge started.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: A papal indulgence campaign to raise money for rebuilding St. Peter's in Rome
options.why: In 1517 preachers such as Johann Tetzel were selling an indulgence proclaimed under Pope Leo X to fund St. Peter's Basilica. This is the money-box preaching that theses 27-28 attack.
options.label: key

options.text: The Council of Trent's decrees reaffirming indulgences and the doctrine of purgatory for Catholics
options.why: The Council of Trent met from 1545 to 1563, decades after the theses of 1517.
options.label: wrong_period

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "A papal indulgence campaign to raise money for rebuilding St. Peter's in Rome". In 1517 preachers such as Johann Tetzel were selling an indulgence proclaimed under Pope Leo X to fund St. Peter's Basilica. This is the money-box preaching that theses 27-28 attack.
"Henry VIII's dissolution of English monasteries and his sale of their lands to the gentry" is incorrect: The dissolution happened in the late 1530s, in England, and had nothing to do with indulgence preaching in Germany in 1517.
"The Peace of Augsburg's grant to German princes of the right to choose their territory's faith" is incorrect: The Peace of Augsburg came in 1555, as a result of the religious conflict that Luther's challenge started.
"The Council of Trent's decrees reaffirming indulgences and the doctrine of purgatory for Catholics" is incorrect: The Council of Trent met from 1545 to 1563, decades after the theses of 1517.
facts: In 1517 Johann Tetzel preached an indulgence in German lands to raise funds for rebuilding St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, under Pope Leo X.
The Peace of Augsburg was concluded in 1555.

design.evidence_quote: so soon as the penny jingles into the money-box, the soul flies out [of purgatory]

items.stem: Criticisms like those in the excerpt most directly influenced which later response by the Catholic Church at its general council held between 1545 and 1563?

options.text: Allowing parish priests to marry so as to answer Protestant attacks on clerical immorality
options.why: Trent upheld clerical celibacy and rejected the Protestant acceptance of married clergy.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Requiring that the Mass and the Bible be offered in vernacular languages instead of Latin
options.why: Trent reaffirmed the Latin Vulgate as the authoritative Bible and kept the Latin Mass.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Trent's decrees curbing financial abuses in the granting of indulgences
options.why: The Council of Trent kept the doctrine of indulgences but condemned the evil gains connected with them and abolished the office of indulgence collectors. This responded to the kind of abuse that theses 27-28 describe.
options.label: key

options.text: Declaring that general church councils hold authority superior to that of the pope himself
options.why: Conciliarism belongs to the era of the Council of Constance (1414-1418). Trent ended by strengthening papal authority.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Trent's decrees curbing financial abuses in the granting of indulgences". The Council of Trent kept the doctrine of indulgences but condemned the evil gains connected with them and abolished the office of indulgence collectors. This responded to the kind of abuse that theses 27-28 describe.
"Allowing parish priests to marry so as to answer Protestant attacks on clerical immorality" is incorrect: Trent upheld clerical celibacy and rejected the Protestant acceptance of married clergy.
"Requiring that the Mass and the Bible be offered in vernacular languages instead of Latin" is incorrect: Trent reaffirmed the Latin Vulgate as the authoritative Bible and kept the Latin Mass.
"Declaring that general church councils hold authority superior to that of the pope himself" is incorrect: Conciliarism belongs to the era of the Council of Constance (1414-1418). Trent ended by strengthening papal authority.
facts: The Council of Trent met in sessions between 1545 and 1563.
In 1562 Trent abolished the office of indulgence collectors, and its 1563 decree on indulgences upheld the doctrine while condemning the abuses and evil gains tied to it.
Trent reaffirmed clerical celibacy and the authority of the Latin Vulgate.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Thesis 28 links the money-box to 'gain and avarice,' the same financial abuse that Trent later moved to stop.
design.evidence_quote: gain and avarice can be increased

"THE REFORMATION was extended and established without arousing any strong reaction among Catholics, or inspiring them with a policy. Under the influence of secular interests, profane literature and art, it was a time of slackness in spiritual life. Religious men, like the Cardinals Egidius, Carvajal, and Campeggio, knew, and acknowledged, and deplored, as sincerely as Adrian VI, the growing defects of the ill-governed Church; and at each Conclave the whole of the Sacred College bound itself by capitulations under oath to put an effective check on the excesses of the court of Rome. But at the Lateran Council the same men who had imposed on Leo the obligation to revoke the indulgences suffered them to be renewed; and those who held the language of Erasmus were confronted by a resisting body of officials for whom reform was ruin. Rome flourished on money obtained from the nations in return for ecclesiastical treasures, for promotion and patronage, for indulgences and dispensations. With the loss of Germany the sources of revenue that remained became more necessary; and it was certain that they would be damaged by reform."

options.text: The Council of Trent reaffirmed the seven sacraments and declared that the Latin Vulgate was the authoritative text of scripture.

options.text: Imperial troops of Charles V sacked Rome in 1527, looting churches and briefly holding Pope Clement VII as a prisoner.

options.text: Ignatius of Loyola founded the Society of Jesus, which built schools and sent missionaries to Asia and the Americas.

options.label: true_but_not_responsive

options.text: Leo X sponsored an indulgence campaign in the German lands to help pay for rebuilding St. Peter's Basilica in Rome.
options.why: The indulgence campaign preached in Germany, which Luther attacked in 1517, moved money from German believers to Rome. That is exactly what Acton describes.
options.label: key

"The Council of Trent reaffirmed the seven sacraments and declared that the Latin Vulgate was the authoritative text of scripture." is incorrect: These are doctrinal decrees of Trent. They do not show Rome profiting from fees and indulgences.

"Ignatius of Loyola founded the Society of Jesus, which built schools and sent missionaries to Asia and the Americas." is incorrect: This is real Catholic Reformation history, but Jesuit schools and missions say nothing about Rome drawing revenue from other countries.
facts: Leo X proclaimed an indulgence to fund the rebuilding of St. Peter's Basilica, preached in Germany by Johann Tetzel.
Luther's Ninety-Five Theses of 1517 attacked this indulgence preaching.

design.evidence_quote: Rome flourished on money obtained from the nations in return for ecclesiastical treasures, for promotion and patronage, for indulgences and dispensations

items.stem: The author's description of a Church weakened by "secular interests, profane literature and art" is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Enlightenment philosophes were spreading deist ideas that questioned revealed religion among educated Europeans.

options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Rival popes in Avignon and Rome were still competing for the loyalty of Europe's monarchs and their clergy.
options.why: The Great Schism ended in 1417, about a century before the events in the excerpt.
options.label: wrong_period

"Rival popes in Avignon and Rome were still competing for the loyalty of Europe's monarchs and their clergy." is incorrect: The Great Schism ended in 1417, about a century before the events in the excerpt.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton links the slackness of the early-sixteenth-century Church to secular interests and to profane literature and art, which points to the Renaissance papacy.
design.evidence_quote: Under the influence of secular interests, profane literature and art, it was a time of slackness in spiritual life.

items.stem: The provisions in the excerpt most directly reflect which of the following developments in English government in the late seventeenth century?

options.text: The abolition of the monarchy and House of Lords in favor of a republic governed by a Lord Protector and his army
options.why: This describes the Interregnum of the 1650s. The 1689 document keeps the monarchy and is presented to William and Mary.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The creation of a democratic system in which all adult men gained the right to vote for members of the House of Commons
options.why: The call for 'free' elections did not widen the franchise. Voting stayed limited to property holders long after 1689.
options.label: overstated

options.text: The establishment of a constitutional monarchy in which the Crown needed Parliament's consent for key powers
options.why: The excerpt makes suspending laws, levying money, and keeping a peacetime army illegal without Parliament's consent. These limits are central to the constitutional monarchy settled after the Glorious Revolution.
options.label: key

options.text: The strengthening of royal prerogative so that the monarch could rule and tax without summoning Parliament for years
options.why: The excerpt calls taxation 'by pretence of prerogative' illegal, so this reverses its meaning.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "The establishment of a constitutional monarchy in which the Crown needed Parliament's consent for key powers". The excerpt makes suspending laws, levying money, and keeping a peacetime army illegal without Parliament's consent. These limits are central to the constitutional monarchy settled after the Glorious Revolution.
"The abolition of the monarchy and House of Lords in favor of a republic governed by a Lord Protector and his army" is incorrect: This describes the Interregnum of the 1650s. The 1689 document keeps the monarchy and is presented to William and Mary.
"The creation of a democratic system in which all adult men gained the right to vote for members of the House of Commons" is incorrect: The call for 'free' elections did not widen the franchise. Voting stayed limited to property holders long after 1689.
"The strengthening of royal prerogative so that the monarch could rule and tax without summoning Parliament for years" is incorrect: The excerpt calls taxation 'by pretence of prerogative' illegal, so this reverses its meaning.
facts: The Bill of Rights of 1689 required parliamentary consent for taxation and for a standing army in peacetime.
The Glorious Revolution of 1688-1689 established a constitutional monarchy in England.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The repeated requirement of Parliament's consent for suspending laws, raising money, and keeping an army shows that the Crown's powers were now limited by Parliament.
design.evidence_quote: without consent of Parliament is illegal

options.text: James II's use of royal authority to suspend laws against Catholics and Protestant dissenters

That is the 'suspending power' the excerpt declares illegal, and the context line ties the document to James's departure.
"The Scottish Covenanters' rebellion against an Anglican-style prayer book imposed by Charles I in 1637" is incorrect: This crisis came half a century earlier and helped cause the Civil War. It had nothing to do with a royal power to suspend laws in 1689.
"The Levellers' demands during the 1640s for a written constitution and the vote for most adult men" is incorrect: The Levellers were a radical movement of the Civil War era. The 1689 settlement did not respond to them, and it did not widen the vote.
"Louis XIV's revocation of the Edict of Nantes and the expulsion of Protestant pastors from France in 1685" is incorrect: This really happened in 1685 and made English Protestants more anxious. But it was a French policy, and the clause is not addressing it.

items.stem: The limits on royal power in the excerpt most clearly contrast with the government of Louis XIV of France, who

options.text: abolished noble privileges and opened all royal offices to men of talent, as Napoleon's reforms later did
options.why: Legal privilege was abolished in the Revolution and Napoleonic era. Louis XIV kept the society of orders in place.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: accepted a written charter drafted by the parlements guaranteeing their judges full freedom of debate
options.why: The French parlements were law courts that Louis XIV restricted. He accepted no such charter, and freedom of debate is a right the excerpt gives the English Parliament.

options.text: shared lawmaking authority with an elected assembly that voted each year on the size of the army
options.why: This describes the English model in the excerpt, not French absolutism under Louis XIV.

options.text: ruled without calling the Estates-General and raised revenue without its consent

"shared lawmaking authority with an elected assembly that voted each year on the size of the army" is incorrect: This describes the English model in the excerpt, not French absolutism under Louis XIV.

Louis XIV ruled personally from 1661 to 1715 and built a large standing army without the consent of a representative assembly.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt requires Parliament's grant for money and its consent for a peacetime army, which sets up the contrast with French rule without a representative body.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim Rousseau makes about the social compact in the excerpt?

options.text: Society functions best when private interests compete freely and the state stays out of the economy
options.why: This resembles Adam Smith's economic thought. The excerpt is about forming a political body, not about markets.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: Each person keeps natural rights to life, liberty, and property that no government may override
options.why: This is Locke's position. Rousseau says each person puts his person and all his power in common, so individuals do not hold back separate rights against the whole.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: A ruler receives absolute power from the people, who then surrender any right to resist him
options.why: This is closer to Hobbes's Leviathan (1651). Rousseau places members under the general will of the whole body, not under one ruler.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: Joining the compact turns separate individuals into one collective body with a shared will
options.why: Rousseau says the act of association replaces each contracting party's individual personality with a moral and collective body that has its own unity and will.
options.label: key

"Each person keeps natural rights to life, liberty, and property that no government may override" is incorrect: This is Locke's position. Rousseau says each person puts his person and all his power in common, so individuals do not hold back separate rights against the whole.
"A ruler receives absolute power from the people, who then surrender any right to resist him" is incorrect: This is closer to Hobbes's Leviathan (1651). Rousseau places members under the general will of the whole body, not under one ruler.

"Frederic at once made himself master of Silesia. There were certain territorial claims. The succession was about to be disputed, and a scramble might be expected. The death of the Russian empress, Anne, made it improbable that Austria would be protected on that side. Frederic was ambitious, and he was strong enough to gratify his ambition. No accepted code regulated the relations between States. It could not be exactly the same as that between men; and in what respect it differed was not determined. States were absolute, and acknowledged no law over them. Grave and disinterested men would have admitted that that may be done for the State which could not be done for the individual; that robbery was not robbery, that murder was not murder, if it was committed in the public interest. There might be a want of generosity, a want of delicacy about it; but if conquest by unprovoked attack was a crime, in the same sense or the same degree as poisoning a man to obtain his property, history must undergo a fundamental revision, and all respect for sovereign authority must be banished from the world."

"Gorbachev’s emphasis on perestroika and glasnost’ domestically and within Eastern Europe was supported to varying degrees by the East European leaders in the midto late 1980s. items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim of the excerpt about Soviet policy toward Eastern Europe in the mid- to late 1980s?

options.text: Moscow still sought strong influence in Eastern Europe but relied less on force to keep it
options.why: The excerpt says the basic policy of keeping a high level of influence was unchanged, but the means shifted from coercion toward political and economic instruments.
options.label: key

options.text: Moscow kept its bloc together mainly by threatening armed intervention like that in Prague in 1968
options.why: The excerpt describes a shift away from coercion, the opposite of reliance on military threats.
options.label: reversal

options.text: All six East European leaders welcomed perestroika and glasnost and copied the Soviet reforms at home
options.why: The excerpt says East Germany, Czechoslovakia, and Romania resisted far-reaching reforms.
options.label: overstated

options.text: Moscow had given up its interest in Eastern Europe and let each bloc state set its own course freely
options.why: The excerpt states the policy of maintaining a high level of influence had not been altered.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Moscow still sought strong influence in Eastern Europe but relied less on force to keep it". The excerpt says the basic policy of keeping a high level of influence was unchanged, but the means shifted from coercion toward political and economic instruments.
"Moscow kept its bloc together mainly by threatening armed intervention like that in Prague in 1968" is incorrect: The excerpt describes a shift away from coercion, the opposite of reliance on military threats.
"All six East European leaders welcomed perestroika and glasnost and copied the Soviet reforms at home" is incorrect: The excerpt says East Germany, Czechoslovakia, and Romania resisted far-reaching reforms.
"Moscow had given up its interest in Eastern Europe and let each bloc state set its own course freely" is incorrect: The excerpt states the policy of maintaining a high level of influence had not been altered.
facts: Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985 and promoted perestroika and glasnost.
Warsaw Pact forces invaded Czechoslovakia in 1968.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The final sentence contrasts the unchanged goal of influence with the changed, less coercive means.
design.evidence_quote: the nature of Soviet influence apparently had shifted away from coercion toward political and economic instruments of influence

items.stem: The Soviet shift away from coercion in Eastern Europe described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Khrushchev's 1956 Secret Speech denouncing Stalin, which ended the use of Soviet troops to control the bloc
options.why: The Secret Speech came decades earlier, and Soviet troops crushed the Hungarian uprising later that same year.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The Maastricht Treaty's creation of the European Union, which drew Warsaw Pact states into Western trade
options.why: The Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1992, after the period the excerpt describes and after the Warsaw Pact dissolved.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The arrival of Marshall Plan aid, which tied East European economies more closely to Western markets and banks
options.why: Marshall Plan aid began in 1948 and was refused by the Soviet bloc under Moscow's pressure.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Soviet economic stagnation, made worse by arms race spending and the costly war in Afghanistan
options.why: By the 1980s the Soviet economy was stagnating and burdened by military spending and the war in Afghanistan (1979-1989), which made coercive control of the bloc more costly and pushed Gorbachev toward reform.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Soviet economic stagnation, made worse by arms race spending and the costly war in Afghanistan". By the 1980s the Soviet economy was stagnating and burdened by military spending and the war in Afghanistan (1979-1989), which made coercive control of the bloc more costly and pushed Gorbachev toward reform.
"Khrushchev's 1956 Secret Speech denouncing Stalin, which ended the use of Soviet troops to control the bloc" is incorrect: The Secret Speech came decades earlier, and Soviet troops crushed the Hungarian uprising later that same year.
"The Maastricht Treaty's creation of the European Union, which drew Warsaw Pact states into Western trade" is incorrect: The Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1992, after the period the excerpt describes and after the Warsaw Pact dissolved.
"The arrival of Marshall Plan aid, which tied East European economies more closely to Western markets and banks" is incorrect: Marshall Plan aid began in 1948 and was refused by the Soviet bloc under Moscow's pressure.
facts: The Soviet Union fought in Afghanistan from 1979 to 1989.
The Soviet economy experienced prolonged stagnation in the 1970s and 1980s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's reference to a move from coercion to political and economic tools under Gorbachev's reform agenda is the development students must place in context.
design.evidence_quote: shifted away from coercion toward political and economic instruments of influence

items.stem: The leaders' support for reform in Poland and Hungary described in the excerpt is most directly connected to which of the following developments in 1989?

options.text: Negotiated change, such as Round Table talks with Solidarity that led to partly free elections
options.why: In Poland, Round Table talks in early 1989 led to the June 1989 elections that Solidarity won, and Hungary also moved toward a negotiated transition; reform-minded leaders made a peaceful handover possible.
options.label: key

options.text: Soviet tanks entering their capitals to crush reformers as they had done in Budapest in 1956 and Prague in 1968
options.why: The USSR did not intervene in 1989, which fits the shift away from coercion the excerpt describes.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Their immediate admission as full members of the European Union and NATO in the same year as the reforms
options.why: Poland and Hungary joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004, not in 1989.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: A violent uprising in which army units joined protesters and the ruling leader and his wife were executed
options.why: This describes Romania in December 1989, a state the excerpt lists among those whose leaders resisted reform.
options.label: misattributed

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Negotiated change, such as Round Table talks with Solidarity that led to partly free elections". In Poland, Round Table talks in early 1989 led to the June 1989 elections that Solidarity won, and Hungary also moved toward a negotiated transition; reform-minded leaders made a peaceful handover possible.
"Soviet tanks entering their capitals to crush reformers as they had done in Budapest in 1956 and Prague in 1968" is incorrect: The USSR did not intervene in 1989, which fits the shift away from coercion the excerpt describes.
"Their immediate admission as full members of the European Union and NATO in the same year as the reforms" is incorrect: Poland and Hungary joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004, not in 1989.
"A violent uprising in which army units joined protesters and the ruling leader and his wife were executed" is incorrect: This describes Romania in December 1989, a state the excerpt lists among those whose leaders resisted reform.
facts: Polish Round Table talks between the government and Solidarity took place in 1989, followed by partly free elections in June 1989.
Nicolae Ceausescu was executed in December 1989.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt names Poland and Hungary as states whose leaders supported Gorbachev's reforms.
design.evidence_quote: The leaders of Poland, Hungary, and Bulgaria apparently supported Gorbachev's reforms
